screens.title: State Management & Navigation in React Native
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we connect two practical pillars of interactive apps: state and navigation. You will learn how state and props control what a component shows and how it behaves, how the useState hook gives functional components local, reactive data, and how useEffect performs one-time or dependency-driven work such as fetching data. We’ll also step through the minimal setup for React Navigation’s Stack Navigator and the standard pattern for passing parameters between screens. The examples you’ll see include a login form that uses controlled TextInput fields, a small data fetch that shows loading and result states, and a two-screen To-Do starter app demonstrating navigation and route parameters. That combination—managing local component state, running side effects safely, and moving between screens—lets you build apps that respond to user input, fetch remote data, and present different views. By the end of this lesson you’ll be able to control inputs with state, schedule effects with useEffect, and wire up a Stack Navigator to pass data between screens.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Overview
State Management & Navigation
Manage interactive data with hooks and move between screens with React Navigation’s Stack.

You will see how props carry immutable values into components, how state is owned and updated using useState, and how useEffect schedules side effects such as network requests. We’ll also show the minimal Stack setup and how to pass parameters when navigating.

In this lesson
State & Props
Why components re-render and how data flows.
Hooks
useState for local data, useEffect for side effects.
Navigation
Stack Navigator and passing params between screens.
Visual Concept
Props
Immutable inputs from the parent. Example: a Button gets title and onPress.
State
Owned by the component and updated with useState to trigger re-render.
Starter pattern
const [value, setValue] = useState('');
// controlled input
<TextInput value={value} onChangeText={setValue} />
Explore Key Topics
useState
Local component state and setter pattern used for inputs and counters.
useEffect
Run side effects like fetching once or when dependencies change.
Navigation
Stack Navigator organizes screens and passes route parameters.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Core Skills
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you will use immediately. First, you will explain state and props: that props are immutable inputs from a parent, and state is local, mutable data a component manages to control its rendered output. Second, you will be able to use the useState hook to add reactive values in a functional component, including the typical pattern of a value and a setter and how that connects to controlled inputs. Both objectives are foundational because they let you build forms, counters, and any UI that changes in response to user actions. For example, a login form uses state to hold the typed username and password while props define a button label passed from a parent. Practice diagnosing whether data belongs in state or props — a common misconception is trying to mutate props inside a child component instead of asking the parent to change them. By the end of these objectives you should be able to choose the right place for a piece of data and implement useState to make components interactive.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Misconceptions
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives emphasize applying hooks correctly and avoiding common pitfalls. You will practice controlled components, where inputs use both value and onChangeText bound to state. A concrete example is the login form that keeps username and password in state and only updates them via their setter functions. You will learn the useEffect dependency array and how an empty array makes an effect run once, while listing variables causes re-run when those variables change. A common misconception is to use useEffect as a replacement for all logic; instead, useEffect is for side effects—things that reach outside the component, like network calls. Finally, you will implement a Stack Navigator and pass parameters during navigation; the destination reads route. params and should defensively check for undefined values. Practicing these patterns will make your components predictable and your navigation robust. You’ll also learn quick checks for bugs: ensure NavigationContainer wraps your navigator and that route. params is present before using it.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Practice & Misconceptions
Controlled Component Pattern
A controlled input uses both a value from state and an onChange handler that updates that state. This ensures a single source of truth for the input value.
Mnemonic
Value + Setter → Controlled
useEffect Dependency Checklist
  • Empty array [] → run once after initial render.
  • Omit array → runs after every render (rarely desired).
  • Include variables → runs when those variables change.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
Quick Navigation Checklist
Ensure NavigationContainer wraps the Stack, install required native modules, and always check route.params for undefined before reading values. Passing params is done with navigation.navigate('Details', { itemId: 86 }).

screens.title: Props vs State
screens.narratorSegment: Let’s define the two fundamental data concepts in React Native: props and state. Props are short for properties and are the immutable inputs a parent component passes to a child. They configure the child: think of a Button that receives a title and an onPress function from a parent. Props should never be changed inside the child; changing them requires the parent to pass new values. State is the component’s own mutable data. A component declares state with useState and updates it via the provided setter. When state changes, React schedules a re-render so the UI reflects the new values. For example, a TextInput that tracks typed text stores that text in state; every keypress calls the setter and re-renders the input with the updated value. A common misconception is to try to update props directly in a child; this leads to unexpected behavior and breaks the unidirectional data flow. Instead, lift state up to a shared parent when multiple children need to see the same data. Think of props as read-only configuration and state as the component’s internal snapshot that evolves over time. How would you decide whether a piece of data belongs in props or state for your next component?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Props are immutable inputs; state is mutable, owned data that triggers re-renders when updated.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Props vs State
Props (Immutable)
Passed from parent to child. Use props to configure a component’s behavior or display without allowing the child to change them directly.
Example: <Button title="Save" onPress={handleSave} />
Common mistake
Trying to mutate a prop inside a child instead of asking the parent to change it.
State (Mutable)
Owned by component and changed with useState. Changing state triggers a re-render to update the UI.
Example: const [text, setText] = useState('');
Pro tip
Lift state up when multiple sibling components need the same data.
Quick comparison
Props: Read-only
State: Read/Write via setters
Flow: Parent → Child

screens.title: useState Hook — TextInput & Login Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson walks through the useState pattern inside a login form, showing how controlled components keep the input value in state. The basic pattern is const [value, setValue] = useState(initial). The TextInput receives value and onChangeText. When onChangeText calls setValue, React schedules a re-render and the new value becomes the rendered input value. Concretely, a login form usually holds username and password in state variables. The submit handler reads those values and performs logic such as validation or calling an authentication A P I. The provided example shows two separate state variables: username and password, each initialized with an empty string, and setters used directly as onChangeText handlers. A useful shorthand is passing the setter directly: onChangeText={setUsername}. A common mistake is leaving a controlled input without a value prop, which makes it uncontrolled and can produce warnings or inconsistent UI. Another error is deriving input display directly from props that never change; instead, local state is appropriate for temporary form values. Practice by adding a small check: do not call the submit action if username or password are empty. How could you extend this pattern to show inline validation messages?

keyIdea.text: useState plus controlled inputs provides a single source of truth for form fields and predictable re-renders.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › useState Login
Example: Login Form (excerpt)
import React, { useState } from 'react';
import { View, TextInput, Button } from 'react-native';

export default function Login() {
  const [username, setUsername] = useState('');
  const [password, setPassword] = useState('');

  const handleLogin = () => {
    if (username === 'user' && password === 'pass') {
      // success
    } else {
      // failure
    }
  };

  return (
    <View>
      <TextInput value={username} onChangeText={setUsername} placeholder="Username" />
      <TextInput value={password} onChangeText={setPassword} placeholder="Password" secureTextEntry />
      <Button title="Login" onPress={handleLogin} />
    </View>
  );
}
Explanation & Tips
  • Pass the setter directly to onChangeText for concise code.
  • Keep inputs controlled by always providing value prop tied to state.
  • Validate before submitting to avoid accidental empty submissions.
Common Mistake

Mixing controlled and uncontrolled inputs causes inconsistent state and warning messages. Always provide value and onChangeText for controlled fields.

Quick Exercise
Add inline validation: if username.trim() === '' show a small message and disable the submit action until both fields are non-empty.

screens.title: useEffect Hook — Side Effects & Dependencies
screens.narratorSegment: useEffect is the standard hook for running side effects in functional components. A side effect is any operation that interacts with the outside world or with APIs that are not part of rendering: fetching data, setting up subscriptions, or manually interfacing with native modules. The effect callback runs after render. By default it runs after every render, but you control that behavior with the dependency array. An empty array makes the effect run only once, similar to componentDidMount. Including variables in the array causes the effect to re-run when those variables change. A typical pattern is to place a data fetch inside useEffect with an empty array so the fetch runs once when the component mounts and then you update state with the fetched data. Be mindful to return a cleanup function from useEffect when you create subscriptions or timers, to avoid leaks. A common misconception is to place heavy synchronous logic in render instead of inside an effect; remember render should be fast and side effects belong in useEffect. When debugging, check the dependency array to ensure the effect runs at the intended times.

keyIdea.title: Claim
keyIdea.text: useEffect runs side effects after render; the dependency array determines when it runs.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › useEffect
useEffect Example (fetch once)
useEffect(() => {
  const fetchData = async () => {
    const response = await fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1');
    const json = await response.json();
    setData(json);
    setLoading(false);
  };

  fetchData();
  return () => { /* cleanup */ };
}, []);
Best Practices
  • Use empty array for component-mount effects like initial data fetch.
  • List dependencies that the effect uses; omit none intentionally.
  • Return cleanup to cancel subscriptions or timers.
Misconception Check
Do not use useEffect to compute derived state synchronously during render. Derived values should be computed directly or memoized. useEffect is for tasks that are intentionally performed after render and are allowed to be asynchronous.

screens.title: Data Fetching Example with useEffect
screens.narratorSegment: Here we step through a typical data fetching pattern using useEffect. Start by creating loading and data state variables with useState. Inside useEffect, define an async function that calls fetch and parses JSON, then set the data and flip loading to false. The empty dependency array ensures the fetch runs only once when the component mounts. While loading is true, render an ActivityIndicator or a loading message. Once the fetch completes, render the data. Add a try/catch around the fetch to handle network errors and set loading false in a finally block. Optionally return a cleanup function that cancels or ignores results if the component unmounts before the fetch resolves—this avoids setting state on an unmounted component. A common mistake is not handling the loading state, which can show an empty UI or produce errors while data is still being fetched. The concrete example uses jsonplaceholder so you can experiment with the response shape and display fields safely. After building this pattern, you will have a reliable template for one-time data fetching inside functional components. Data Fetching Example with useEffect means fetch in useeffect with loading and error state; clean up or guard updates if unmounted.. In practical terms, loading states, async fetch, and cleanup pattern. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Fetch in useEffect with loading and error state; clean up or guard updates if unmounted.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Data Fetching
Fetch pattern (excerpt)
const [data, setData] = useState(null);
const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);

useEffect(() => {
  let mounted = true;
  const fetchData = async () => {
    try {
      const resp = await fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1');
      const json = await resp.json();
      if (mounted) setData(json);
    } catch (e) {
      console.error(e);
    } finally {
      if (mounted) setLoading(false);
    }
  };
  fetchData();
  return () => { mounted = false; };
}, []);
UI states
  • Show loading indicator while loading is true.
  • Show data when available; show an error message when fetch fails.
  • Guard state updates if the component unmounts before fetch completes.
Concrete example output
Fetched Data: use the json response's title or id to render a summary. This gives a predictable user experience during asynchronous loads.

screens.title: Installing and Configuring React Navigation
screens.narratorSegment: React Navigation is the standard library for handling navigation in React Native. The minimal setup includes installing @react-navigation/native, installing native dependencies for screens and safe areas, and then installing the stack package. After installation you wrap your app with NavigationContainer which manages the navigation state, then create a Stack using createStackNavigator and define screens inside Stack. Navigator. Each Stack. Screen has a name and component. The navigation prop is automatically injected into screen components so you can call navigation. navigate(name, params) to move between screens, navigation. goBack() to return, or navigation. popToTop() to return to the first screen. A common setup error is forgetting to wrap the navigator inside NavigationContainer which results in navigation props not working. Also ensure native dependencies like react-native-screens and react-native-safe-area-context are installed and linked correctly. This simple process gives you push and pop behavior similar to a web history stack, and it is ideal for apps with hierarchical screens like a list and detail view. What two things will you check first if navigation calls fail in your app? Installing and Configuring React Navigation means install navigation packages, wrap the app in navigationcontainer, and define screens with createstacknavigator.. In practical terms, minimal setup steps for stack navigator in a react native app. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Setup steps
keyIdea.text: Install navigation packages, wrap the app in NavigationContainer, and define screens with createStackNavigator.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › React Navigation Setup
Install packages (commands)
Example install steps you will run in your project shell:
npm install @react-navigation/native expo install react-native-screens react-native-safe-area-context npm install @react-navigation/stack
Minimal App code
import { NavigationContainer } from '@react-navigation/native';
import { createStackNavigator } from '@react-navigation/stack';

const Stack = createStackNavigator();

function App() {
  return (
    <NavigationContainer>
      <Stack.Navigator>
        <Stack.Screen name="Home" component={HomeScreen} />
        <Stack.Screen name="Details" component={DetailsScreen} />
      </Stack.Navigator>
    </NavigationContainer>
  );
}
Checklist & Troubleshooting
  • Wrap the navigator in NavigationContainer.
  • Confirm native dependencies are installed and linked.
  • Check that screen components receive navigation and route props.

screens.title: Stack Navigator — Navigation Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Stack Navigator models screens as a stack of pages: pushing a screen places it on top, and popping removes the top screen returning to the previous one. This is ideal for flows like a list to details. The navigation prop provides methods such as navigate(name, params) to push a named screen, goBack() to pop one level, and popToTop() to return to the root. When you navigate and pass parameters, you include an object as the second argument, for example navigation. navigate('Details', { itemId: 86 }). The destination receives these parameters via route. params and should defensively check them. A common mistake is reading route. params without a fallback, which can produce undefined errors. Architecturally, place navigation logic in screens rather than deeply nested components; if a nested component needs navigation, pass a callback from the screen or use useNavigation hook carefully. For complex apps, combine stack navigators with tabs or drawers; but for many apps, a single Stack Navigator for hierarchical navigation is sufficient. Consider which parts of your UI should be pushed as separate screens versus shown inline to keep navigation simple and predictable.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Stack Navigator Patterns
Common Methods
  • navigation.navigate('ScreenName', params) — push a screen and pass params.
  • navigation.goBack() — pop one level.
  • navigation.popToTop() — return to the first screen.
Parameter Passing Example
Call: navigation.navigate('Details', { itemId: 86, otherParam: 'anything' }); Destination reads: const { itemId, otherParam } = route.params;
Design advice
Use stack navigation for hierarchical flows. Keep navigation simple: avoid passing large objects as params; pass IDs or small payloads and fetch larger data on the destination if needed.

screens.title: To-Do App Starter — Home Screen
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson follows the provided To-Do starter code that creates a two-screen app. On the Home screen, you manage a todoText and todos array with useState. When the Add To-Do button is pressed, the addTodo function checks that the input is non-empty, appends the new item to the todos array, and clears the input. A FlatList maps over todos to render each item. To navigate to the details screen, call navigation. navigate('Details', { totalItems: todos. length }). That shows a practical example of combining state and navigation: the number of items is derived from local state and passed as a parameter during navigation. Beware of mutating the existing array directly; always create a new array when updating state, for example setTodos([... todos, newItem]) to ensure React detects the change. Also ensure keyExtractor is stable, using the index only when items have no unique id, knowing that indices can produce slightly unstable keys when items are reordered or removed. This Home screen is a compact demonstration of state, controlled inputs, and passing derived data to another screen via navigation parameters. To-Do App Starter — Home Screen means manage list state with usestate and pass a derived parameter (todos.length) when navigating to a details screen.. In practical terms, using usestate to manage a list and navigate with parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › To-Do Home
Starter snippet (HomeScreen)
function HomeScreen({ navigation }) {
  const [todoText, setTodoText] = useState('');
  const [todos, setTodos] = useState([]);

  const addTodo = () => {
    if (todoText.trim().length > 0) {
      setTodos([...todos, todoText.trim()]);
      setTodoText('');
    }
  };

  // Render FlatList and navigate with todos.length
}
Notes & Checks
  • Use setTodos([...todos, newItem]) to avoid mutating state.
  • Clear the input after adding to improve UX.
  • Pass totalItems: todos.length when navigating to Details.
Exercise
Extend the Home screen to prevent adding duplicate items and show a small message when the list is empty.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › To-Do Details
DetailScreen pattern
function DetailScreen({ route, navigation }) {
  const totalItems = route.params ? route.params.totalItems : 0;

  return (
    <View>
      <Text>To-Do List Details</Text>
      <Text>Total items: {totalItems}</Text>
      <Button title="Go back" onPress={() => navigation.goBack()} />
    </View>
  );
}
This defensive pattern ensures your screen renders sensibly when params are absent. Prefer small primitive params and re-fetch larger data when necessary.

screens.title: Common Mistakes & Debugging Checklist
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson lists common mistakes and how to diagnose them. For state: mutating arrays or objects directly prevents React from detecting changes. Always create new arrays or objects when updating state. For useEffect: omitting the dependency array or forgetting dependencies leads to effects running at unintended times or stale closures. If an effect runs too often, check the dependencies and memoize functions or values if necessary. For navigation: forgetting NavigationContainer, not installing native dependencies, or misnaming screen names will break navigation. Also, reading route. params without a fallback is a common source of runtime errors. Concrete debugging steps include: look for console warnings about controlled versus uncontrolled inputs, verify that setters are called with expected values, add logs inside useEffect to track when it runs, and confirm navigation props exist on the screen component. When a data fetch fails, show an error state to the user and log the exception to the console to capture network issues. These checks will accelerate finding and fixing common issues. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we connect two practical pillars of interactive apps: state and navigation. You will learn how state and props control what a component shows and how it behaves, how the useState hook gives functional components local, reactive data, and how useEffect performs one-time or dependency-driven work such as fetching data. We’ll also step through the minimal setup for React Navigation’s Stack Navigator and the standard pattern for passing parameters between screens. The examples you’ll see include a login form that uses controlled TextInput fields, a small data fetch that shows loading and result states, and a two-screen To-Do starter app demonstrating navigation and route parameters. That combination—managing local component state, running side effects safely, and moving between screens—lets you build apps that respond to user input, fetch remote data, and present different views. By the end of this lesson you’ll be able to control inputs with state, schedule effects with useEffect, and wire up a Stack Navigator to pass data between screens.

These objectives map to practical skills you will use immediately. First, you will explain state and props: that props are immutable inputs from a parent, and state is local, mutable data a component manages to control its rendered output. Second, you will be able to use the useState hook to add reactive values in a functional component, including the typical pattern of a value and a setter and how that connects to controlled inputs. Both objectives are foundational because they let you build forms, counters, and any UI that changes in response to user actions. For example, a login form uses state to hold the typed username and password while props define a button label passed from a parent. Practice diagnosing whether data belongs in state or props — a common misconception is trying to mutate props inside a child component instead of asking the parent to change them. By the end of these objectives you should be able to choose the right place for a piece of data and implement useState to make components interactive.

These objectives emphasize applying hooks correctly and avoiding common pitfalls. You will practice controlled components, where inputs use both value and onChangeText bound to state. A concrete example is the login form that keeps username and password in state and only updates them via their setter functions. You will learn the useEffect dependency array and how an empty array makes an effect run once, while listing variables causes re-run when those variables change. A common misconception is to use useEffect as a replacement for all logic; instead, useEffect is for side effects—things that reach outside the component, like network calls. Finally, you will implement a Stack Navigator and pass parameters during navigation; the destination reads route. params and should defensively check for undefined values. Practicing these patterns will make your components predictable and your navigation robust. You’ll also learn quick checks for bugs: ensure NavigationContainer wraps your navigator and that route. params is present before using it.

Let’s define the two fundamental data concepts in React Native: props and state. Props are short for properties and are the immutable inputs a parent component passes to a child. They configure the child: think of a Button that receives a title and an onPress function from a parent. Props should never be changed inside the child; changing them requires the parent to pass new values. State is the component’s own mutable data. A component declares state with useState and updates it via the provided setter. When state changes, React schedules a re-render so the UI reflects the new values. For example, a TextInput that tracks typed text stores that text in state; every keypress calls the setter and re-renders the input with the updated value. A common misconception is to try to update props directly in a child; this leads to unexpected behavior and breaks the unidirectional data flow. Instead, lift state up to a shared parent when multiple children need to see the same data. Think of props as read-only configuration and state as the component’s internal snapshot that evolves over time. How would you decide whether a piece of data belongs in props or state for your next component?

This lesson walks through the useState pattern inside a login form, showing how controlled components keep the input value in state. The basic pattern is const [value, setValue] = useState(initial). The TextInput receives value and onChangeText. When onChangeText calls setValue, React schedules a re-render and the new value becomes the rendered input value. Concretely, a login form usually holds username and password in state variables. The submit handler reads those values and performs logic such as validation or calling an authentication A P I. The provided example shows two separate state variables: username and password, each initialized with an empty string, and setters used directly as onChangeText handlers. A useful shorthand is passing the setter directly: onChangeText={setUsername}. A common mistake is leaving a controlled input without a value prop, which makes it uncontrolled and can produce warnings or inconsistent UI. Another error is deriving input display directly from props that never change; instead, local state is appropriate for temporary form values. Practice by adding a small check: do not call the submit action if username or password are empty. How could you extend this pattern to show inline validation messages?

useEffect is the standard hook for running side effects in functional components. A side effect is any operation that interacts with the outside world or with APIs that are not part of rendering: fetching data, setting up subscriptions, or manually interfacing with native modules. The effect callback runs after render. By default it runs after every render, but you control that behavior with the dependency array. An empty array makes the effect run only once, similar to componentDidMount. Including variables in the array causes the effect to re-run when those variables change. A typical pattern is to place a data fetch inside useEffect with an empty array so the fetch runs once when the component mounts and then you update state with the fetched data. Be mindful to return a cleanup function from useEffect when you create subscriptions or timers, to avoid leaks. A common misconception is to place heavy synchronous logic in render instead of inside an effect; remember render should be fast and side effects belong in useEffect. When debugging, check the dependency array to ensure the effect runs at the intended times.

Here we step through a typical data fetching pattern using useEffect. Start by creating loading and data state variables with useState. Inside useEffect, define an async function that calls fetch and parses JSON, then set the data and flip loading to false. The empty dependency array ensures the fetch runs only once when the component mounts. While loading is true, render an ActivityIndicator or a loading message. Once the fetch completes, render the data. Add a try/catch around the fetch to handle network errors and set loading false in a finally block. Optionally return a cleanup function that cancels or ignores results if the component unmounts before the fetch resolves—this avoids setting state on an unmounted component. A common mistake is not handling the loading state, which can show an empty UI or produce errors while data is still being fetched. The concrete example uses jsonplaceholder so you can experiment with the response shape and display fields safely. After building this pattern, you will have a reliable template for one-time data fetching inside functional components. Data Fetching Example with useEffect means fetch in useeffect with loading and error state; clean up or guard updates if unmounted.. In practical terms, loading states, async fetch, and cleanup pattern. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

React Navigation is the standard library for handling navigation in React Native. The minimal setup includes installing @react-navigation/native, installing native dependencies for screens and safe areas, and then installing the stack package. After installation you wrap your app with NavigationContainer which manages the navigation state, then create a Stack using createStackNavigator and define screens inside Stack. Navigator. Each Stack. Screen has a name and component. The navigation prop is automatically injected into screen components so you can call navigation. navigate(name, params) to move between screens, navigation. goBack() to return, or navigation. popToTop() to return to the first screen. A common setup error is forgetting to wrap the navigator inside NavigationContainer which results in navigation props not working. Also ensure native dependencies like react-native-screens and react-native-safe-area-context are installed and linked correctly. This simple process gives you push and pop behavior similar to a web history stack, and it is ideal for apps with hierarchical screens like a list and detail view. Stack Navigator models screens as a stack of pages: pushing a screen places it on top, and popping removes the top screen returning to the previous one. This is ideal for flows like a list to details. The navigation prop provides methods such as navigate(name, params) to push a named screen, goBack() to pop one level, and popToTop() to return to the root. For complex apps, combine stack navigators with tabs or drawers; but for many apps, a single Stack Navigator for hierarchical navigation is sufficient. Consider which parts of your UI should be pushed as separate screens versus shown inline to keep navigation simple and predictable.

These three key concepts are the ones to carry forward. First, props are immutable inputs from parent components that configure children; never try to mutate them inside a child. Second, state is mutable data owned by the component; use useState to declare state and its setter and use controlled inputs to ensure a single source of truth. Third, useEffect runs side effects after render; control its execution with the dependency array and return a cleanup function when needed. Each of these patterns has common pitfalls we covered: attempting to change props in children, mixing controlled and uncontrolled inputs, and forgetting dependencies or cleanups in effects. Remembering these core concepts will help you build predictable, debuggable React Native components and to structure navigation and data flows appropriately. A final set of practical reminders: React Navigation’s Stack Navigator gives you push and pop behavior; always wrap your app in NavigationContainer and check that navigation props are available. When passing parameters, use an object as the second argument to navigation. navigate and access them safely with route. params in the destination. For data fetching, manage loading and error states and guard against updating state after unmount by returning cleanup from useEffect or using a mounted flag. Lastly, prefer passing small identifiers or counts as navigation params rather than large data structures; fetch or recompute larger payloads on the destination screen when necessary. These practical patterns reduce bugs, improve memory usage, and keep your navigation predictable as your app grows.
